content.title: Tangents and Chords of Circles: Geometric Properties and Angle Relationships
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the core geometric properties of tangents and chords in a circle. On the SAT, understanding the perpendicular relationship between a tangent and a radius, the perpendicular bisector property of chords, and the tangent segments theorem is key to solving complex geometry problems.
learning_objectives: Identify and apply the property that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.
Use the property that a perpendicular line from the center to a chord bisects the chord.
Apply the theorem that two tangent segments from a single external point to a circle are equal in length.
Combine the Pythagorean theorem with circle properties to solve right triangle problems involving tangents, chords, and radii.

sections.title: Core Properties of Tangents
sections.content: A tangent is a line that intersects a circle at exactly one point. There are two critical SAT concepts regarding tangents: 1. Perpendicularity: A tangent line is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency. This means the angle between the tangent and the radius is always 90 degrees. 2. Tangent Segments Theorem: Tangent segments from the same external point to a circle are equal in length. This often creates an isosceles triangle or two congruent right triangles when connected to the center.

sections.title: Geometric Characteristics of Chords
sections.content: A chord is a line segment connecting any two points on a circle. 1. Perpendicular Bisector Property: If a line from the center of the circle is perpendicular to a chord, it bisects that chord. 2. Constructing Right Triangles: By connecting the center, the midpoint of the chord, and one endpoint of the chord, a right triangle is formed. In this triangle, the two legs are half the chord length and the distance from the center to the chord (apothem), while the hypotenuse is the radius.

sections.title: Integrated Applications of Tangents and Chords
sections.content: When dealing with figures containing tangents and chords, it is usually necessary to add auxiliary lines (such as radii) to reveal right triangles. Using the Pythagorean theorem ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$) is the standard procedure for finding unknown segment lengths. For example, if the tangent length and radius are known, the distance from the center to the external point can be calculated.

worked_examples.question: Circle O has a radius of 5. Line L is tangent to circle O at point P. Point A lies on line L such that AP = 12. Find the distance from point A to the center O.
worked_examples.solution: 1. According to tangent properties, radius OP is perpendicular to tangent L, so triangle OPA is a right triangle with a 90-degree angle at P. 2. Given leg OP = 5 (radius) and leg AP = 12 (tangent segment). 3. Use the Pythagorean theorem: $OA^2 = OP^2 + AP^2 = 5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169$. 4. Take the square root: $OA = 13$. Therefore, the distance from point A to the center is 13.

worked_examples.question: In a circle with a radius of 10, there is a chord with a length of 16. Find the perpendicular distance from the center to this chord.
worked_examples.solution: 1. Let the center be O, the chord be AB, and M be the midpoint of chord AB. 2. According to the perpendicular bisector theorem, OM is perpendicular to AB, and $AM = MB = 16 / 2 = 8$. 3. Connect OA to form right triangle OMA. The hypotenuse OA = 10 (radius) and leg AM = 8. 4. Use the Pythagorean theorem: $OM^2 + AM^2 = OA^2$, which is $OM^2 + 8^2 = 10^2$. 5. $OM^2 + 64 = 100$, so $OM^2 = 36$. 6. Take the square root: $OM = 6$. The distance from the center to the chord is 6.

common_mistakes: Incorrectly assuming a tangent and a chord are always perpendicular; in reality, only the radius at the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent.
Forgetting to divide the chord length by 2 when calculating chord problems (i.e., using the full length instead of the half-length to form a right triangle).
Confusing the tangent segment length (distance from the point to the point of tangency) with the distance from the point to the center of the circle.
exam_tips: When you see a tangent, immediately draw the radius connecting the center to the point of tangency and mark the 90-degree right angle symbol.
When you see a chord, you usually need to draw a perpendicular line from the center to the chord to construct a right triangle using the perpendicular bisector property.
Pythagorean triples (such as 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17) appear frequently on the SAT; memorizing these can speed up your problem-solving.
content.recap: Master the three major theorems: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius, a perpendicular from the center bisects a chord, and tangent segments from an external point are equal. By constructing right triangles with the radius as the hypotenuse and applying the Pythagorean theorem, most circle-related segment and angle calculations can be solved.

knowledge_claims.content: A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.
A tangent is a line that has exactly one point in common with a circle.
Tangent segments from the same external point to a circle are equal in length.
If a line from the center of a circle is perpendicular to a chord, then it bisects the chord.
In chord length calculations, a right triangle is typically constructed using the radius, half the chord, and the distance from the center to the chord.
In a tangent triangle, the radius $r$, tangent segment $s$, and distance from the center to the external point $d$ satisfy $r^2 + s^2 = d^2$.
It is an error to use the full chord length instead of the half-chord length in the Pythagorean theorem for chord problems.
If a line is perpendicular to a radius at its endpoint on the circle, then the line is tangent to the circle.
A tangent intersects a circle at one point, whereas a secant intersects a circle at two points.
When verifying tangent problems, check that the constructed triangle uses the radius and tangent segment as the legs.
